title: Managers and Managerial Roles
tagline: Mintzberg’s ten roles, the authority–responsibility–accountability chain, delegation against decentralisation, and leading change.

overview.intro: A manager is measured not by how much work she personally does but by what gets done through other people. This unit first sets out what a manager does by examining Mintzberg’s observed roles, then covers the foundation of managerial power in authority, responsibility and accountability, then the two ways work is passed downward in delegation and decentralisation, and finally change itself: why organisations resist it and the two models the syllabus expects for leading it, Lewin’s three-step model and the ADKAR model. The through-line is that authority without accountability is unsafe, and change without a method is merely disruption.

facts.label: Mintzberg’s roles
facts.value: Ten roles in three groups: interpersonal (figurehead, leader, liaison), informational (monitor, disseminator, spokesperson), decisional (entrepreneur, disturbance handler, resource allocator, negotiator).

facts.label: Delegation vs decentralisation
facts.value: Delegation passes a task while accountability stays put; decentralisation spreads decision-making authority across the organisation as a policy.

facts.label: Change models
facts.value: Lewin: unfreeze, change, refreeze. ADKAR: awareness, desire, knowledge, ability, reinforcement.

facts.label: Exam weight
facts.value: Mintzberg’s roles, delegation against decentralisation and the change models are recurring theory questions.

learningOutcomes: Describe Mintzberg’s managerial roles and group them correctly.
Explain authority, responsibility and accountability and their relationship.
Distinguish delegation from decentralisation on the accepted grounds.
Explain Lewin’s three-step model of change management.
Apply the ADKAR model to a change situation.

blocks.text: Henry Mintzberg studied what managers actually do rather than what the classical texts said they should do, and found that the job is characterised by brevity, variety and fragmentation, with communication carrying much of the workload. He identified ten roles arranged in three groups. The interpersonal group arises from the manager’s formal authority and status: as figurehead she performs symbolic duties such as signing and greeting, as leader she motivates and directs subordinates, and as liaison she maintains a network of contacts outside her unit.

blocks.caption: Mintzberg’s ten managerial roles
rows: Performs symbolic and legal duties: signing documents, receiving visitors
Maintains a network of contacts inside and outside the unit
Seeks and receives information to understand the unit’s environment
Passes information from outsiders or subordinates to members of the unit
Transmits information to outsiders about the organisation
Initiates and supervises projects and improvements
Responds to unexpected crises and conflicts
Decides who gets what: budget, time, staff
Represents the unit in negotiations with other parties

blocks.text: The informational roles follow from the interpersonal ones: a manager who meets many people receives information first, so she monitors the environment, disseminates what she learns inside the team, and speaks for the unit outside it. The decisional roles then convert that information into action: she starts initiatives, handles disturbances, allocates resources and negotiates.

items.text: A plant manager signs a delivery receipt for a new machine.
items.note: Figurehead: the act is symbolic and legal, and could be delegated in substance but not in status.

items.text: The same manager reassigns two staff to a breakdown on the line.
items.note: Disturbance handler and resource allocator acting together, which is how the roles overlap in practice.

blocks.text: Authority is the legitimate right to give orders and expect compliance, flowing downward from a formal position in the organisation. Responsibility is the obligation of the subordinate to perform the duty assigned to it, and it arises only when authority is delegated. Accountability is the answerability for the proper performance of the duty, and it flows upward: a person remains accountable to the superior who delegated the work. The three travel together, and the discipline of management lies in never separating them, because authority without accountability is abuse and responsibility without authority is unfair.

blocks.caption: Authority, responsibility and accountability compared
rows: Never: it stays with the person

items: Authority is delegated, not owned personally; it comes with the post.
Responsibility follows the work and must be matched by enough authority to do it.
Accountability cannot be delegated: the manager remains answerable even after delegating.
Over-delegation of authority without clarity of responsibility produces drift.
Responsibility without adequate authority produces frustration and delay.

blocks.text: Delegation is the assignment of a specific task to a subordinate together with the authority to perform it, while accountability for the result remains with the delegator. It is a one-to-one act between a superior and a subordinate and it ends when the task is complete. Decentralisation is a deliberate policy of dispersing decision-making authority throughout the organisation, so that routine decisions are made at the levels closest to the action. It is permanent, organisation-wide and affects the structure, whereas delegation is a day-to-day management act.

blocks.caption: Delegation against decentralisation
rows: Assignment of a task with authority
Dispersal of decision-making authority as policy
Ends when the task is done
Shared with the lower level for its decisions

blocks.text: Delegation has three elements: assignment of duty, granting of matching authority, and creating accountability. Its advantages are that it relieves the superior of routine work, develops subordinates, speeds decisions and enables quicker action at the point where information lives. Its limitations are the reluctance of managers to delegate, the risk of abuse of authority, and the preference of some subordinates to avoid responsibility.

items.text: A branch manager authorises a teller to approve loans up to a stated limit.
items.note: Delegation: authority passes for a defined purpose, while the branch manager remains accountable for every approval.

items.text: A retail chain lets each store fix staffing rosters within a policy framework.
items.note: Decentralisation: a standing dispersal of authority built into the structure rather than a one-off task.

blocks.text: Change management is the process of moving an organisation from its present state to a desired future state with the least resistance and the greatest durability. Kurt Lewin’s model gives three steps. Unfreeze creates the readiness for change by showing why the current method is no longer viable, often by making the cost of staying the same visible. Change is the transition itself, where new methods are introduced and people learn them. Refreeze stabilises the new way by embedding it in policy, training and reward, so that the organisation does not drift back to old habits.

ADKAR, developed by Jeff Hiatt, works on the individual rather than the process, and holds that organisational change happens only when each person passes five sequential gates: Awareness of the need for change, Desire to participate and support it, Knowledge of how to change, Ability to implement the required skills and behaviours, and Reinforcement to make the change stick. A failure at any one gate stalls the whole transition, which makes the model a useful diagnostic: if people know what to do but will not do it, the problem is desire, not training.

blocks.caption: Lewin’s three steps against ADKAR’s five gates
rows: Create readiness by showing the need
Introduce and learn the new method
Stabilise the new method in systems

items: Resistance usually comes from fear of the unknown, loss of status, or doubt about the evidence.
Communicate the reason early and specifically rather than in generalities.
Involve the people affected, because participation reduces resistance.
Train before requiring performance, so that ability keeps pace with expectation.
Reinforce with appraisal, reward and updated procedure, or the change decays.

keyPoints: Mintzberg identified ten managerial roles in interpersonal, informational and decisional groups.
The figurehead role performs symbolic and legal duties rather than operational ones.
The leader role motivates and directs subordinates, which is distinct from the figurehead role.
Authority is the right to give orders and flows downward from a formal position.
Responsibility is the obligation to perform and arises when authority is delegated.
Accountability is answerability, flows upward, and can never be delegated.
Delegation is a one-to-one act that ends with the task; decentralisation is a structural policy.
Delegation’s three elements are assignment of duty, matching authority and accountability.
Lewin’s model is unfreeze, change, refreeze.
ADKAR is awareness, desire, knowledge, ability, reinforcement, applied to each individual.
examFocus: Mintzberg questions are marked on grouping: give the role and say which group it belongs to.
In delegation answers, state explicitly that accountability stays with the delegator, since that is the point examiners look for.
Change-model answers should apply the model to the scenario given rather than reciting the steps in the abstract.

vocabulary.meaning: Categories of behaviour a manager is expected to perform, as identified by Mintzberg.
Legitimate right arising from a formal position to give orders and expect compliance.
Obligation of a subordinate to perform the duty assigned to her.
Answerability for the proper performance of a task, which cannot be delegated.
Assignment of a specific task with the authority needed to perform it.
Policy of dispersing decision-making authority throughout the organisation.
Individual change model of awareness, desire, knowledge, ability and reinforcement.

questions.prompt: Which group of Mintzberg’s roles includes the leader and the figurehead?
questions.explanation: The interpersonal roles arise directly from the manager’s formal authority and status within the unit.

questions.prompt: The role of spokesperson belongs to which group of Mintzberg’s roles?
questions.explanation: Transmitting information to outsiders about the organisation is an informational role, following from the contacts the manager holds.

questions.prompt: Which of the following can NEVER be delegated?
questions.explanation: A manager who delegates work remains answerable for the result, so accountability stays permanently with the delegator.

questions.prompt: A firm that allows each regional office to make its own purchasing decisions as a standing policy is practising:
questions.explanation: A permanent, organisation-wide dispersal of decision-making authority is decentralisation, not a one-off delegation.

questions.prompt: The three steps of Lewin’s model of change are unfreeze, change and __________ .
questions.explanation: Refreeze stabilises the new method in policy and reward so that the organisation does not return to its old habits.

questions.prompt: The first gate of the ADKAR model, which makes people understand why the change is needed, is __________ .
questions.explanation: Without awareness of the need for change the remaining four gates cannot begin, because there is no reason to proceed.

questions.prompt: Explain authority, responsibility and accountability with the direction in which each flows.
questions.answer: Authority is the legitimate right to give orders, arising from a formal position, and it flows downward. Responsibility is the obligation to perform the assigned duty, created when authority is delegated, and it also flows downward. Accountability is answerability for proper performance, flows upward to the person who delegated, and can never itself be delegated.
questions.explanation: All three definitions are needed along with the direction of flow, which is what distinguishes a complete answer.

questions.prompt: Give three differences between delegation and decentralisation.
questions.answer: First, scope: delegation is an act between one superior and one subordinate, while decentralisation is an organisation-wide policy. Second, duration: delegation ends when the task is complete, whereas decentralisation is permanent and built into the structure. Third, accountability: in delegation the delegator remains fully accountable, while in decentralisation the lower level becomes accountable for the decisions it is authorised to take.
questions.explanation: Three bases of comparison are required, each stated as a contrast rather than a description of one of the two.

questions.prompt: Explain Lewin’s three-step model of change management with an example at each step.
questions.answer: Lewin’s model holds that change must be prepared, carried out and then stabilised. Unfreeze creates readiness for change by showing why the present method is no longer viable; for example a retailer publishes falling footfall figures so staff understand why the online channel must be introduced. Change is the transition itself, where the new method is introduced and learned, for example staff are trained to take and fulfil online orders for a trial period. Refreeze stabilises the change by embedding it in procedure, appraisal and reward, for example the online order process is written into the standard operating procedure and included in performance targets. Without refreezing the organisation drifts back to the previous practice once the pressure of the project is removed.
questions.explanation: Full marks require all three steps with the purpose of each and a worked example that fits the step rather than a generic illustration.

questions.prompt: A hospital is introducing a new electronic patient-record system. Senior doctors are resisting, ward staff say they are too busy to learn it, and no one has explained why the change is happening. Apply the ADKAR model and state what the management should do at each gate.
questions.answer: Awareness is missing because the reason has never been explained, so management must communicate the specific case: fewer transcription errors, faster retrieval and a legal requirement to keep records electronically. Desire is weak because senior doctors see no personal benefit and some loss of status, so they must be involved in choosing the configuration and given influence over the rollout schedule. Knowledge is absent because no training has been scheduled, so structured sessions must run before go-live rather than after. Ability is limited by time pressure on ward staff, so protected time, super-users on each shift and a simplified interface must be provided. Reinforcement is entirely missing, so the new system must be written into policy, used in appraisal, and supported by switching off the paper process, since a parallel system guarantees the old habit survives. The five gates must be worked in order, because a later gate cannot compensate for an earlier failure.
questions.explanation: The answer is marked on diagnosing which gate has actually failed in the scenario and prescribing the matching intervention, not on reciting the five letters.
